lyrics:
They clocked the hour, they logged the weight
Counted fingers, closed the file
A paper tag pinned to the crate
Stamped "as expected" with a smile

Down the hall some other kid
came in loud and came in bent
screaming everything he did
while they smoothed me, called it meant

Default settings — before a name
they kept the box but lost the guide
No one checked if I'd turn out the same
and called it me, though it lied

They wheeled me past the nursery floor
and drove me somewhere I'd call home
No one had met me there before —
just someone's son, already grown

Default settings — before a name
they kept the box but lost the guide
No one checked if I'd turn out the same
and called it me, though it lied

Nobody reads the settings twice
Nobody thinks to ask them why
I was already running
the second I opened my eyes

Default settings — before a name
they kept the box but lost the guide
No one checked if I'd turn out the same
and called it me, though it lied

impression.text: This upbeat pop-rock track exudes a bright and nostalgic atmosphere, driven by a high-energy funk groove. The production is exceptionally clean and polished, featuring a dense arrangement where punchy horn lines and a vibrant slap bass sit perfectly beneath the smooth male lead vocals. A standout moment occurs halfway through when a soaring electric guitar solo bursts into the mix, elevating the emotional intensity before seamlessly transitioning back into the catchy vocal hook. The tight rhythm section maintains a bouncy, infectious feel throughout the entire song, making the overall sound both sophisticated and highly danceable.

review.review_text: The conceit here is cold-blooded and Rose knows it: a birth described as a factory intake report, "A paper tag pinned to the crate / Stamped 'as expected' with a smile." The Canterbury-scene machinery does the emotional work the deadpan vocal refuses to, all interlocking organ and Rhodes clicking along at a brisk 152 in E minor, and that mid-song guitar break bursts the clinical spell open just when the wryness starts to calcify. The best line is the quietest one, the bridge admission that "I was already running / the second I opened my eyes," which turns the whole software-metaphor gag into something that actually stings. Not quite the knockout that the Zappa-drunk sprawl of "Wazoo in Effigy" was, but it's a clever machine that earns its wit; this one lands cleanly.
